subject: Accounting
title: Direct vs. Indirect Costs
description: A quick, practical guide to Direct vs. Indirect Costs.

hook.text: The flour in a loaf of bread is a direct cost. The bakery's electricity bill is indirect.

buildup.text: Direct costs can be traced to a specific product—materials, labor on that item.

discovery.text: Indirect costs (overhead) benefit many products—rent, insurance, management salaries.

twist.text: Allocating overhead to products is tricky. Different methods give different costs per unit.

climax.text: Getting the split right determines which products appear profitable and which don't.

punchline.text: Direct costs are obvious. Indirect costs hide everywhere.

quiz.question: What is an indirect cost?
options: A cost that benefits many products and can't be traced to one
The raw material in a product
A cost paid directly to suppliers

details.summary: Direct costs can be traced to a specific product or department; indirect costs cannot and must be allocated. This topic explains the distinction, provides common examples of each, and shows why the classification matters for product costing and pricing.
details.whyItMatters: Correctly classifying costs as direct or indirect determines how accurately products are costed. Misclassification leads to products being priced too high or too low, hurting competitiveness or profitability.
takeaways: Direct costs like raw materials and production labor are easily traced to specific products
Indirect costs like factory rent and utilities benefit multiple products and require allocation
The same cost can be direct in one context and indirect in another depending on the cost object

faq.question: What is the difference between direct and indirect costs?
faq.answer: Direct costs can be traced to a specific product, project, or department—like the lumber used to build a table. Indirect costs benefit multiple cost objects and must be allocated—like the electricity powering the entire factory.

faq.question: Why does it matter whether a cost is classified as direct or indirect?
faq.answer: Direct costs are assigned precisely to the products that consume them, while indirect costs are spread across products using estimation. Misclassifying a direct cost as indirect (or vice versa) distorts product costs and leads to poor pricing and profitability analysis.
